lines: One microservice just went down.

lines.text: So why are ten others failing?

lines: A downstream service stops responding.
But the caller keeps calling, and retrying.
Every call holds a thread, waiting on a timeout.
The threads run out, and the failure cascades upstream.
scenes.label: THE PROBLEM

lines: The fix is a circuit breaker.
It wraps the call and watches for failures.
Too many, and it stops calling the failing service, giving it time to recover.
scenes.label: THE FIX

lines: Closed: requests flow normally, while the breaker tracks the failure rate.

lines.text: Cross the threshold, say fifty percent, and it trips open.

lines: Now calls fail instantly, without ever touching the service.

lines.text: After a wait period, it goes half-open, and lets a few trial requests through.

lines: If they fail, it opens again.
scenes.label: HOW IT WORKS

lines: Picture a checkout.
The order service calls payments, and payments calls the bank.
Then the bank's API goes down.

lines.text: The breaker opens, and payments returns a fallback: payment pending, we'll retry.

lines: Orders keep flowing.
scenes.label: IN PRODUCTION

lines: Without it: retries, exhausted threads, and a cascading failure.
With it: requests fail fast, fall back, and the system stays stable.
scenes.label: BEFORE vs AFTER

lines: For interviews, remember three things.
One. It stops cascading failures.
Two: closed, open, half-open.
Three: pair it with timeouts and a fallback.
scenes.label: INTERVIEW NOTES

lines.text: A circuit breaker stops calling what's broken, so everything else keeps working.

lines: Follow for more system design, explained visually.
And save this for your next interview.
